lectures.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome
lectures.deck: CMS I Obstructive Sleep Apnea & Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome - Shah Fallsv.pptx
lectures.note: Built from the slides. Lecture 39 (Phases of Sleep) has no disease and so no Clin Med Pro card. The STOP-Bang questionnaire is a picture on slide 17. Where the slides give two neck sizes (17 and 16 inches by sex as a risk factor; 16 inches for anyone on STOP-Bang) each is kept with its own tool. The apnea-hypopnea severity bands are in the speaker notes only and are left out. Dosing is left out.

fields.name: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)
fields.definition: Sleep-disordered breathing from upper airway narrowing: obstructive apneas (no airflow despite continued respiratory effort; airflow down 90% or more for at least 10 seconds) and hypopneas (slowed, shallow breathing in episodes of 10 seconds or longer)
fields.etiology: Narrowing of the upper airway by excessive soft tissue or structural abnormalities
fields.epidemiology: The most common form of sleep-disordered breathing; prevalence increases with age; sleep-disordered breathing is more common after menopause than before
fields.risk_factors: Obesity, macroglossia, micrognathia, retrognathia, neck circumference 17 inches or more (men) or 16 (women), enlarged tonsils, increasing age, male sex, family history, alcohol or sedatives, hypothyroidism
fields.pathology: Upper airway collapse during sleep while effort continues; untreated: increased sympathetic tone, bradycardia, blood pressure variability, arrhythmias, raised C-reactive protein, cortisol and proinflammatory cytokines
fields.clinical: Daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, witnessed apnea, snorting or gasping awakenings, loud habitual snoring, morning headache, nocturia, poorly controlled hypertension, poor concentration, low libido, night sweats; exam: obesity, large neck, enlarged tonsils, crowded posterior oropharynx
fields.diagnosis: Split-night or all-night polysomnogram (gold standard); 5 or more predominantly obstructive events per hour plus a symptom, or 15 or more events, not explained by another condition; apnea-hypopnea and respiratory disturbance indices; thyroid-stimulating hormone if hypothyroidism is suspected; home kits assess only obstructive apnea and may miss mild disease, so use a polysomnogram with significant cardiopulmonary disease, neuromuscular weakness, awake hypoventilation or hypoxemia, stroke, long-term opioids, severe insomnia or a suspected non-obstructive sleep disorder; STOP-Bang (snoring, tired, observed, pressure, body mass index over 35, age over 50, neck 16 inches, gender male) preoperatively, not for community screening
fields.treatment: Continuous positive airway pressure (most effective); autotitrating pressure without significant comorbidities; positional therapy; oral appliance (not severe disease, not without teeth); nasal expiratory device; stimulants (modafinil or armodafinil; caution with cardiovascular, hepatic, psychiatric disease; lower doses in the elderly); nasal steroids; surgery (tracheostomy is a cure); weight loss; avoid alcohol and sedatives; refer to a sleep physician
fields.mortality: Untreated: 2.5 times the driving accidents, 3 to 6 times the risk of sudden cardiac death at night, high heart failure mortality, 3 times the risk of hypertension; pulmonary hypertension, stroke, insulin resistance and diabetes, arrhythmias, ischemic heart disease, fatty liver (2 to 3 times), reflux (75 to 100%); lower mortality in the elderly, who compensate

fields.name: Central sleep apnea (CSA)
fields.definition: Sleep-disordered breathing in which the brainstem stops sending signals to breathe: no airflow and no respiratory effort
fields.etiology: Increased sensitivity to carbon dioxide causing unstable breathing, hyperventilation alternating with apnea; in heart failure, Cheyne-Stokes breathing from a prolonged circulation delay to the carotid chemoreceptors
fields.epidemiology: Less common than obstructive sleep apnea
fields.risk_factors: Congestive heart failure, stroke, opioid medications, hypoxia, high altitude, use of continuous positive airway pressure
fields.pathology: Airflow stops because respiratory effort is absent or decreased (in obstructive apnea the airway collapses while effort continues)
fields.clinical: Insomnia, frequent awakenings, nocturnal dyspnea, nonrestorative sleep, daytime sleepiness; snoring less common than in obstructive apnea; sounds very similar to obstructive apnea
fields.diagnosis: Polysomnography (home testing not sufficient): repetitive apneas without thoracic-abdominal excursion
fields.treatment: Treat the cause (optimize heart failure therapy, reduce opioids, descend from altitude); continuous positive airway pressure first; adaptive servo-ventilation if it fails, avoided especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), Pickwickian syndrome
fields.definition: Awake alveolar hypoventilation (raised awake arterial carbon dioxide) in an obese person that cannot be attributed to another condition; a diagnosis of exclusion
fields.etiology: Obesity with reduced lung function and reduced inspiratory muscle strength; severe obstructive sleep apnea may be present (70% have severe obstructive symptoms)
fields.epidemiology: More likely as body mass index rises; patients may present in their 50s and 60s; male sex is not a risk factor; 90% have coexisting obstructive apnea symptoms (70% severe), 10% coexisting sleep hypoventilation (older women)
fields.risk_factors: Central obesity (high waist-to-hip ratio), reduced lung function from obesity, reduced inspiratory muscle strength, severe obstructive sleep apnea
fields.pathology: Awake hypoventilation with hypercapnia; late disease: hypoxemic hypercapnic respiratory failure and right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension
fields.clinical: Nonspecific: obese (body mass index over 30) and hypersomnolent, loud snoring, choking, fatigue, poor memory, small oropharynx, thick neck, dyspnea on exertion, facial plethora, elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, pedal edema
fields.diagnosis: Screen when awake saturation is 94% or less or the overnight lowest is below 80%, or with unexplained dyspnea, right heart failure, facial plethora or a raised bicarbonate (over 27: get an arterial blood gas). Diagnose: body mass index over 30, awake arterial carbon dioxide over 45 mm Hg, other causes excluded; labs (metabolic panel, blood count, thyroid, pulmonary function, chest film, toxicology); gold standard polysomnography with continuous nocturnal carbon dioxide monitoring
fields.treatment: Multidisciplinary; first line weight loss plus continuous positive airway pressure (with obstructive apnea) or bilevel positive airway pressure (with sleep hypoventilation) and lifestyle change; second line tracheostomy with nocturnal ventilation, bariatric surgery, medications after diet and exercise fail; refer to a sleep specialist
fields.mortality: High morbidity and mortality; progresses untreated; cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; more hospital and intensive care use; poor prognosis with significant awake hypoxemia at diagnosis

lectures.title: Inflammatory Lung Diseases
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the lecturer's narrated recording, which only chooses which facts to star. Slides 72-74 (acute respiratory distress syndrome) are AI-made pictures with typos; the plateau pressure figure on slide 74 ('under 50 cm H2O') is left out. He said not to memorize the cause and drug charts and that the rare idiopathic subtypes are not test material. Dosing is left out.

conditions.name: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
conditions.prof_note: He called idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis "kind of the most common thing"; the four over-65 criteria allow a diagnosis without a surgical lung biopsy.

fields.name: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), usual interstitial pneumonia
fields.definition: The most common idiopathic (fibrosing) interstitial pneumonia: pulmonary fibrosis with no associated cause
fields.etiology: Unknown; smoking is the cause in the majority of cases
fields.epidemiology: [[★ The most common subtype of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia]], itself the most common diagnosis among patients with interstitial lung disease; 67 to 75% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and familial lung fibrosis have smoked; the four criteria that make a surgical lung biopsy unnecessary apply over 65
fields.risk_factors: Smoking (67 to 75% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and familial lung fibrosis have smoked; smoking is the cause in the majority of cases)
fields.pathology: As in all fibrosis: inflammatory cells gather in the alveolar walls, alveolitis drives fibroblast production and collagen causes the fibrosis; CT shows diffuse, patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing
fields.clinical: Insidious dry cough, exertional dyspnea, fatigue and malaise; clubbing, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, tachypnea, reduced chest expansion
fields.diagnosis: Restrictive pattern (normal or increased ratio, decreased lung volumes); chest film with progressive fibrosis over several areas; CT with diffuse patchy fibrosis and pleural-based honeycombing; lavage or biopsy as needed. Over 65 with idiopathic disease and crackles, restrictive physiology, progressive fibrosis over years and honeycombing on high-resolution CT: 90% confidence, no surgical lung biopsy needed
fields.treatment: Controversial: nothing has improved survival or quality of life compared with no treatment; smoking cessation is critical
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Idiopathic (fibrosing) interstitial pneumonias
fields.definition: Interstitial pneumonias of unknown cause defined by histopathologic pattern
fields.etiology: Unknown
fields.epidemiology: Taken together the most common diagnosis among interstitial lung diseases; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common subtype
fields.risk_factors: Smoking (67 to 75% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and familial lung fibrosis have smoked)
fields.pathology: Patterns: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, desquamative interstitial pneumonitis, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia, acute interstitial pneumonitis
fields.clinical: Dry cough, exertional dyspnea, constitutional symptoms; symptoms vary by subtype
fields.diagnosis: Suspect in unexplained interstitial lung disease; may require biopsy; age, sex, prodrome, imaging and histology together
fields.treatment: Depends on the subtype; corticosteroids may be used in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia), lymphoid and nonspecific interstitial pneumonia
fields.mortality: Prognosis depends on the subtype diagnosed

conditions.name: Pulmonary fibrosis with connective tissue disease

fields.name: Pulmonary fibrosis associated with connective tissue disorders
fields.definition: An inflammatory and fibrotic interstitial response in autoimmune (connective tissue) disease
fields.etiology: Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome, polymyositis-dermatomyositis, scleroderma; methotrexate, used to treat many of them, has been implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: The underlying autoimmune disease; methotrexate therapy
fields.pathology: Inflammatory and fibrotic lung response
fields.clinical: The general interstitial lung disease picture (no slide specific to connective tissue disease): progressive exertional dyspnea, persistent nonproductive cough; crackles, clubbing
fields.diagnosis: High antinuclear antibody (collagen vascular disease); restrictive pulmonary function; imaging
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Sarcoidosis
conditions.prof_note: "Sarcoid, you could see questions about"; lupus pernio with a dry cough is a red flag; know the lab clues and the stages.

fields.name: Sarcoidosis
fields.definition: A multi-organ disease of idiopathic cause with noncaseating granulomatous inflammation, most often of the lungs and lymphatic system
fields.etiology: Unknown; environmental triggers (viral, bacterial, mycobacterial, inhaled agents, mold) in a genetically predisposed person
fields.epidemiology: Granulomatous lung inflammation in about 90%; higher in North American Black and Northern European white people; more often women; onset in the third and fourth decades
fields.risk_factors: Genetic predisposition plus environmental exposure
fields.pathology: Noncaseating granulomas (T lymphocytes, macrophages, epithelioid cells) in lungs, nodes, eyes, skin, liver, spleen, salivary glands, heart, nervous system
fields.clinical: Cough, insidious dyspnea, chest discomfort, malaise, fever, weakness, weight loss, nontender lymphadenopathy; erythema nodosum, parotid enlargement, hepatosplenomegaly, crackles, [[★ lupus pernio (painful skin sores on the face)]]
fields.diagnosis: Chest film: symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy, stages I to IV; [[★ elevated sedimentation rate and angiotensin-converting enzyme (40 to 80%)]], hypercalcemia (5%), hypercalciuria, eosinophilia, leukopenia; transbronchial or fine-needle node biopsy with noncaseating granulomas confirms; biopsy is essential whenever findings suggest an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma
fields.treatment: About 90% respond to corticosteroids (indications: disabling constitutional symptoms, hypercalcemia, iritis, uveitis, arthritis, central nervous system or cardiac involvement, granulomatous hepatitis, skin lesions other than erythema nodosum, progressive pulmonary lesions); methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab if intolerant or refractory; yearly exam, pulmonary function, chest film, electrocardiogram, chemistry and eye exam
fields.mortality: Best with hilar adenopathy alone; parenchymal involvement is worse; 20% with lung involvement develop irreversible impairment (fibrosis, bronchiectasis, cavitation)

fields.name: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (a pneumoconiosis)
fields.definition: Chronic fibrotic lung disease from inhaled coal dust
fields.etiology: Inhaled coal dust taken up by alveolar macrophages, forming coal macules
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Coal dust exposure
fields.pathology: Coal macules; complicated disease is progressive massive fibrosis (conglomeration of the upper lungs)
fields.clinical: Simple disease usually asymptomatic; complicated: progressive dyspnea, inspiratory crackles, clubbing, cyanosis
fields.diagnosis: Restrictive pulmonary function with reduced diffusing capacity; chest film with nodular opacities in the upper lung fields (coal macules 2 to 5 mm)
fields.treatment: Supportive, no curative treatment: oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccines, rehabilitation, smoking cessation; lung transplant in severe cases
fields.mortality: Progressive massive fibrosis: conglomeration and contraction in the upper lung fields

conditions.name: Asbestosis (and mesothelioma)
conditions.prof_note: He said ferruginous bodies (which slide 55 ties to inorganic dust and significant exposure) should make you think asbestos; smoking markedly raises the lung cancer risk.

fields.name: Asbestosis
fields.definition: Interstitial fibrosis of the terminal bronchioles, alveoli and interstitium from inhaled asbestos fibers that cannot be removed
fields.etiology: Asbestos fibers from insulation, demolition, shipyards and construction
fields.epidemiology: Exposure over 10 to 20 years; patients usually seek attention about 15 years after exposure
fields.risk_factors: Asbestos exposure; cigarette smoking increases radiographic changes and markedly increases lung carcinoma
fields.pathology: Chronic inflammation and macrophage invasion form fibrosis; fibers can reach the pleura and cause mesothelioma; [[★ ferruginous bodies in tissue suggest significant exposure]]
fields.clinical: Dyspnea on exertion, rarely cough; fine bibasilar crackles and clubbing with progression
fields.diagnosis: Labs not helpful; reduced vital capacity and total lung capacity; imaging often normal early; pleural plaques the most common chest film finding, basal reticulonodular opacities; CT preferred (plaques, alveolitis, fibrosis, honeycombing)
fields.treatment: Supportive: oxygen, physiotherapy, medications, vaccinations
fields.mortality: Increased lung cancer and mesothelioma, especially in smokers; mesothelioma (pleural, nearly always from asbestos, 10% lifetime risk in asbestos workers) is incurable with poor survival, diagnosed by pleural fluid cytology

conditions.name: Silicosis
conditions.prof_note: A thick, milky lavage is "usually confirmatory"; screen for tuberculosis.

fields.name: Silicosis
fields.definition: Fibrosis and nodular lung lesions from free crystalline silica dust (silicon dioxide)
fields.etiology: Silica dust from mining, sandblasting, quarry work and stone work
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Silica exposure
fields.pathology: Silica deposits in the alveoli cause chronic inflammation, macrophage invasion, fibrosis and nodules, mostly in the upper lobes (a lighter dust); complicated disease conglomerates the upper lungs
fields.clinical: Simple disease usually asymptomatic (slide 60); dyspnea, cough, weight loss, fatigue; crackles. Slide 61 also says "rapid onset of symptoms": the two slides differ on onset
fields.diagnosis: Arterial blood gas; reduced forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in 1 second; [[★ bronchoalveolar lavage: thick, milky effluent with foamy, lipoproteinaceous macrophages]]; silicotic nodules 1 to 10 mm and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes
fields.treatment: Largely supportive: oxygen, physiotherapy, medications, vaccinations, smoking cessation; [[★ tuberculosis skin test and a current chest film]]. (Slide 54, in the coal section, adds that corticosteroids may relieve the chronic alveolitis in silicosis)
fields.mortality: Increased risk of tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis, scleroderma

conditions.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
conditions.prof_note: "Find the agent, avoid the agent"; reversible if caught early.

fields.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis)
fields.definition: A non-atopic, non-asthmatic inflammatory lung disease caused by inhaled organic material
fields.etiology: Organic dusts: moldy hay (farmer's lung), bird excreta and feathers (bird fancier's lung), cheese maker's lung, moldy sugarcane pulp, insect-infested grain
fields.epidemiology: Acute after exposure; subacute in 15% and chronic in 5%, after multiple exposures
fields.risk_factors: Repeated exposure to the organic agent
fields.pathology: Interstitial lymphocytes and plasma cells with noncaseating granulomas; fibrosis with continued exposure
fields.clinical: Sudden malaise, chills, fever, cough, dyspnea, nausea 4 to 8 hours after exposure (may mimic paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea); bibasilar crackles, tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis; chronic: fatigue, weight loss, fibrosis, clubbing
fields.diagnosis: Serum antibodies to the agent (definitive); white count elevated with a left shift; hypoxia; restrictive function; little imaging change acutely, later small nodular densities sparing the apices and bases; biopsy if subacute or chronic
fields.treatment: [[★ Identify and avoid the agent]]; corticosteroids in severe cases; other immunosuppressants; oxygen, bronchodilators, pain medication; lung transplant
fields.mortality: Symptoms can be reversible if caught early; continued exposure may worsen the disease

conditions.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
conditions.prof_note: The most narration time of the lecture: a feared complication of sepsis, trauma, aspiration and more.

fields.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
fields.definition: Acute non-cardiogenic lung injury: within 7 days of a known insult, bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules, failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload, arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio under 300 mm Hg
fields.etiology: Direct: aspiration of gastric contents, diffuse pneumonia, lung contusion, toxic gas, near-drowning, high altitude, radiation, upper airway obstruction, fat, air, amniotic fluid or thrombus emboli. Systemic: sepsis, severe pancreatitis, shock, nonthoracic trauma, overdoses (opioids, aspirin, phenothiazine, tricyclic antidepressants, cocaine), multiple transfusions, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cardiopulmonary bypass, protamine, chemotherapy, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin
fields.epidemiology: About one-third of cases first present with sepsis
fields.risk_factors: The direct and systemic insults above
fields.pathology: Cytokine damage to capillary endothelium and alveolar epithelium; increased permeability, surfactant loss, alveolar collapse and refractory hypoxemia; hyperinflammatory phenotype (high interleukin-6, soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor) with multiorgan failure
fields.clinical: Profound dyspnea 12 to 48 hours after the insult; tachypnea, labored breathing, intercostal retractions, crackles; hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen; multiple organ failure
fields.diagnosis: Bilateral infiltrates becoming confluent, air bronchograms in about 80%, normal heart size with few effusions; echocardiography excludes cardiogenic edema; severity by arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio (mild 200 to 300, moderate 100 to 200, severe under 100 mm Hg); differential: cardiogenic edema, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, severe bilateral pneumonia, autoimmune lung disease
fields.treatment: Treat the precipitant; low tidal volume ventilation; titrate positive end-expiratory pressure (arterial oxygen above 60 mm Hg); early prone positioning in moderate to severe disease; conservative fluids; transfuse at hemoglobin 7 g/dL; corticosteroids conditionally within 14 days; sedatives, analgesics, antipyretics; avoid oscillatory ventilation and routine pulmonary artery catheters; neuromuscular blockade controversial; extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as salvage
fields.mortality: About 30% mortality with low tidal volume ventilation; 20% after trauma to 80% with end-stage liver disease; lung function improves over 6 to 12 months; residual diffusion deficits, weakness and fatigue

lectures.title: Pulmonary Nodules and Neoplasms
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the Zoom recording of the live lecture, which only chooses which facts to star; slide 49 (“Things to Know”) is his own exam list. He said not to memorize the Fleischner tables, the probability-of-malignancy tables, the staging charts in detail, the genes, drugs by marker or the small cell follow-up schedule, so those are summarized or left out. Points the slides state two ways are given both ways or not stated: adenocarcinoma’s share (slides 4 and 31 give different percentages; it is kept as the most common type), stage 3 treatment (slide 35’s text against its table), immunotherapy for squamous cell (slides 37 and 38 against slide 40), the slide 46 “central” and “peripheral” tags on the neurologic syndromes (slide 47 places Lambert-Eaton at the neuromuscular junction), pleural contact as a benign sign (slide 16 against slide 32) and where most lung cancers form (slide 9 against slide 30). The slide 35 survival-by-stage column (never narrated) and dosing are left out. Current guidelines screen younger patients with fewer pack-years than slide 18; the slide’s criteria are kept. The slides give carcinoid tumors, the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone and hypercalcemia no workup or treatment, and none is added.

conditions.name: Pulmonary nodule
conditions.prof_note: “Magic number is 6. Greater than 6 millimeters, I’m suspicious … Especially if I’ve got a spiculated appearance”; a benign nodule’s look, what makes a nodule worrying and the screening criteria are on his slide 49 exam list.

fields.name: Pulmonary nodule (a solitary nodule on a chest X-ray is a coin lesion)
fields.definition: A nodule seen on a chest X-ray or chest computed tomography; a solitary nodule on a chest X-ray is sometimes called a coin lesion. Most are benign, but some are the start of a cancer
fields.etiology: Most are benign: a granuloma (inflammatory) or a hamartoma (connective tissue growth); some are the start of lung cancer
fields.epidemiology: Found incidentally when a chest X-ray or chest computed tomography is done for another reason; most are benign
fields.risk_factors: For malignancy: a patient at high risk of lung cancer (smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancers), whose nodule is worked up to exclude malignancy
fields.pathology: Concerning: [[★ greater than 6 mm]], upper lobes or hilar structures, [[★ spiculated (spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border)]], more than 3 nodules, enlarging over time, contrast enhancing on computed tomography, cavitated or nonsolid, a patient at high risk; ground-glass (stippled) or eccentric calcification. Benign: well-defined borders, fat (hamartoma), diffuse, central, popcorn (hamartoma) or concentric calcification, close to a fissure. On computed tomography: a smooth nodule with fat and calcification (hamartoma), a smooth nodule with central calcification (healed granuloma), an opacity beside the minor fissure (linear scar or lymphoid tissue)
fields.clinical: Usually none: an incidental finding. Persistent cough, hemoptysis, dysphagia, wheezing or shortness of breath, or systemic symptoms (weight loss, fever or fatigue, bone or chest pain, endocrine disorders) call for a lung cancer workup instead
fields.diagnosis: First estimate the size (under 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is high risk). Chest X-ray is not a good tool beyond first spotting it; computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen, then biopsy (bronchoscopy, transthoracic or thoracoscopic, by location; can be guided by computed tomography); positron emission tomography (high uptake suggests malignancy, low or normal uptake is a good sign, inflammation can also take it up). A new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm: assess the clinical probability of malignancy. Screening, for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule: [[★ ages 55 to 80, at least a 30 pack-year history, smoking now or quit within the last 15 years]], with a low-dose chest computed tomography every year. The Fleischner Society tables (2017) guide follow-up of incidental nodules (he said not to memorize them)
fields.treatment: By the probability of malignancy (new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm): very low, computed tomography surveillance at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months; low to moderate, positron emission tomography (negative or mild uptake: the same surveillance; moderate or intense uptake: nonsurgical biopsy or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection); high, staging, then video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection if no metastases are found. Refer (pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist) for a high probability or moderate to intense uptake. A single solid nodule under 6 mm in a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up
fields.mortality: Most nodules are benign. Screening finds cancer early (rapid intervention, better prognosis) but has many false positives that lead to unnecessary workups with complications such as a biopsy

conditions.name: Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma)
conditions.prof_note: His slide 49 list covers screening, staging and how it changes treatment, central versus peripheral types and the paraneoplastic signs. “By the time you get symptoms, we’re way late in the game”: in a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease the symptoms can pass for an exacerbation.

fields.name: Lung cancer (bronchogenic carcinoma): small cell and non-small cell lung carcinoma
fields.definition: Malignancies arising from the lung’s epithelial cells. Two main types: small cell lung carcinoma (oat cell) and non-small cell lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma); mixed and rare types include carcinoid tumors, bronchial gland carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma and Pancoast tumors
fields.etiology: Carcinogens (or other causes of genetic mutation) activate oncogenes, and further mutations or loss of regulatory control inactivate tumor-suppressing genes; smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of cases (second-hand smoke 20%)
fields.epidemiology: More than 200,000 new cases a year in the United States and 2 million worldwide; most occur over 50 years old, but [[★ about 4% under 40, so it stays on the differential]]. Small cell is 15 to 20% of lung cancers; adenocarcinoma is the most common type, squamous cell 20 to 30%, large cell 9 to 10%
fields.risk_factors: Smoking (85 to 90% of cases; second-hand smoke 20%), the risk compounding with packs per day and years (5x to 10x to 20x); radiation and radon; air pollution; environmental and chemical toxins; tuberculosis or human immunodeficiency virus infection; genetics; diet; alcohol intake
fields.pathology: Atypical epithelial cells proliferate and grow into the bronchial lumen, along the mucosa or into the bronchial wall and parenchyma: hyperplasia, dysplasia, in situ cancer, invasive malignancy entering blood and lymph, then metastases. Spread is to regional lymph nodes and distant organs (liver, brain, bone) through angiogenesis and loss of differentiation. [[★ Small cell and squamous cell are central; adenocarcinoma and large cell are peripheral]]. Neuroendocrine cells lining the bronchioles are where the paraneoplastic syndromes start
fields.clinical: [[★ Often no symptoms until the disease is advanced or metastatic]]. Persistent cough, hemoptysis, dysphagia, wheezing or shortness of breath; weight loss, fever or fatigue, bone or chest pain, endocrine disorders. Metastases with no respiratory symptoms: brain (headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncope, seizures; papilledema with raised intracranial pressure; cranial nerve findings near the midbrain or pons), liver (dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, poor appetite, jaundice, hepatic failure), bone (pain, fractures without falls, even from a cough; spinal cord compression), adrenal insufficiency (fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia with hyperkalemia). Paraneoplastic: endocrine (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, hypercalcemia), neurologic (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, with progressive weakness particularly in the legs; cerebellar degeneration or encephalitis), dermatologic (acanthosis nigricans, dermatomyositis), hematologic
fields.diagnosis: Screening (no symptoms, no known nodule): [[★ ages 55 to 80, at least a 30 pack-year history, smoking now or quit within the last 15 years: a low-dose chest computed tomography every year]]. Workup: chest X-ray is not a good tool; computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen, then biopsy (bronchoscopy, transthoracic or thoracoscopic); positron emission tomography; genetic testing; complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium, alkaline phosphatase, pulmonary function tests; sputum cytology (not sensitive). Staged once computed tomography (location and size), positron emission tomography (lymph involvement) and biopsy (tumor type) are back, by tumor, node and metastasis: [[★ a bigger tumor, nodes further away and metastasis are each worse]]; mediastinal or contralateral nodes (N2 or N3) make it stage 3; spread to the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, or outside the chest makes it stage 4 (4A one site outside the chest, 4B several)
fields.treatment: Non-small cell: [[★ stages 1 to 2 surgical resection if the patient can tolerate it; stage 4 chemotherapy]]. Small cell: [[★ chemotherapy and radiation, to which it responds better than the non-small cell types]], with prophylactic cranial irradiation. Unfit for surgery: radiotherapy or ablation. Referral to a pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist
fields.mortality: The highest cancer mortality in men (more than 30% of male cancer deaths) and more than 25% of female cancer deaths; one of the lowest five-year survivals, 17 to 18% in the United States (worse in the rest of the world), because symptoms come only once it is advanced or metastatic

conditions.name: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
conditions.prof_note: On his slide 49 list: how staging changes treatment, big picture only (“do we do surgery? Do we do chemo? … Do you need to know every circumstance? No. Like, big picture, guys”). He said not to learn specific drugs by marker: “Your job as a primary care PA … is be able to screen and figure out risk for that patient, and then refer.”

fields.name: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma
fields.definition: The non-small cell lung carcinomas, divided by histology into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma
fields.etiology: As for lung cancer: oncogenes activated and tumor-suppressing genes inactivated; molecular and genomic testing of the tumor looks for specific mutations and proteins (for example TP53, tumor protein 53, a tumor-suppressor gene that lets cancer grow when damaged)
fields.epidemiology: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer, squamous cell 20 to 30% and large cell 9 to 10%; usually over 50 with a smoking history
fields.risk_factors: Smoking (the strongest association is squamous cell; adenocarcinoma occurs without it too); the general lung cancer risk factors
fields.pathology: [[★ Adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are peripheral; squamous cell carcinoma is central]], often arising in a bronchus; mixed types exist (adenosquamous)
fields.clinical: Respiratory symptoms first (cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, hemoptysis, fatigue); later bone pain, weight loss and paraneoplastic issues
fields.diagnosis: Computed tomography, positron emission tomography and biopsy with histology, then tumor, node and metastasis staging; a mucicarmine stain shows mucin in adenocarcinoma (negative may point to large cell); sputum cytology can catch squamous cell; tumor genetic testing helps the oncologist tailor therapy
fields.treatment: Surgical resection by size and lymph involvement (wedge or segment resection, lobectomy, pneumonectomy; open or thoracoscopic) if the patient can tolerate it (survive and recover). [[★ Stages 1 to 2: surgical resection; stage 4: chemotherapy]], with surgery only for a solitary metastasis with a resectable primary (for stage 3 the slide’s text and its table differ). Chemotherapy and radiation are adjuncts, or for stage 4, because non-small cell cancers respond poorly to them; chemotherapy and immunotherapy can be targeted to genetic and protein markers (gene-marker targeted therapy is for non-squamous disease); checkpoint-inhibitor monoclonal antibodies (the “-mab” drugs) for some patients by marker, by response to standard treatment, or when not a surgical candidate. Unfit for lobectomy: anatomical segmentectomy; unfit for surgery: stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or conventional radical radiotherapy
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Adenocarcinoma of the lung
conditions.prof_note: His board pointer, said three times: “Adenocarcinoma, large cell, usually periphery”; he circled the peripheral spiculated nodule on slide 32.

fields.name: Adenocarcinoma of the lung (a non-small cell lung cancer)
fields.definition: A non-small cell carcinoma usually arising from type II pneumocytes by way of atypical adenomatous hyperplasia; described as noninvasive, minimally invasive or invasive
fields.etiology: Type II pneumocytes (the cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant) are usually the origin, starting as atypical adenomatous hyperplasia
fields.epidemiology: The most common lung cancer; usually over 50 with a smoking history, but smoking is not always associated
fields.risk_factors: Smoking (not always present); frequently associated with peripheral scars
fields.pathology: [[★ Mid-lung and periphery]]. Grows in situ first, then by lepidic growth along the alveolar lining or by invading the stroma (minimally invasive); later it may invade the pleura and vessels or form its own vasculature (invasive). Initial metastases are to the lymphatics before it leaves the lungs; a mucicarmine stain shows its mucin
fields.clinical: Mostly asymptomatic early; persistent cough and shortness of breath without signs of infection; respiratory symptoms first (cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, hemoptysis, fatigue); later bone pain, weight loss and systemic (paraneoplastic) issues
fields.diagnosis: Computed tomography: a peripheral spiculated nodule (on slide 32 it involved the pleura and proved an invasive adenocarcinoma); histology with a positive mucicarmine stain (mucin)
fields.treatment: As for non-small cell lung cancer: surgical resection for stages 1 to 2, chemotherapy for stage 4; targeted therapy and immunotherapy by genetic and protein markers
fields.mortality: Two-thirds present only with advanced disease (T2 or higher with N1 to N3 nodes) or metastatic disease

conditions.name: Large cell carcinoma
conditions.prof_note: “Large cell tends to met to the gut. Small intestine, bowel … that’s specific to large cell, so I would say stuff that, like, is unique to a thing makes a great test question.”

fields.name: Large cell carcinoma of the lung (a non-small cell lung cancer)
fields.definition: A non-small cell carcinoma of exclusion: no specific genetic or histology markers; anaplastic, undifferentiated and pleomorphic, with cells about 3 times larger than baseline
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 9 to 10% of lung cancers
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Anaplastic, undifferentiated, pleomorphic cells about 3 times larger than baseline (kept apart from small cell because their treatments differ); subtypes giant-cell (sarcomatoid), basaloid, rhabdoid and neuroendocrine; [[★ forms in the periphery]]; necrosis and hemorrhage more readily than other non-small cell types; angiogenesis (its own blood supply)
fields.clinical: Metastasis to rare sites such as [[★ the small intestine and bowel]]
fields.diagnosis: Computed tomography: a large, cavitated mass, typically peripheral (unlike the central squamous cell carcinoma), with angiogenesis; biopsy with histology must still confirm it (a large amount of anaplastic tissue); a negative mucicarmine stain may point to it
fields.treatment: No standardized treatment, because of its variety and rarity
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
conditions.prof_note: On his slide 49 list (“how to recognize squamous cell from the others”): “Cavitation is big with that one. Strongest association with smoking … Cough, wheezing, hemoptysis are huge”; it can look like a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease patient “constantly in exacerbation”; “your squamous cell will make your calcium, a big deal.”

fields.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (a non-small cell lung cancer)
fields.definition: A non-small cell carcinoma in a central location, often originating in the bronchus, with frequent cavitation and obstructive phenomena
fields.etiology: Smoking: its association is the strongest of any lung cancer type
fields.epidemiology: The second most common lung cancer (20 to 30%)
fields.risk_factors: [[★ Smoking, the strongest association of any type]]
fields.pathology: [[★ Central, often arising in a bronchus]]; frequent cavitation and obstruction; spreads by local invasion and by lymphangitic spread into the regional (hilar) lymph nodes
fields.clinical: Silent until it obstructs the bronchus, then [[★ cough, wheezing and hemoptysis]]; a large obstruction brings atelectasis and pneumonia; local invasion brings dysphagia and voice changes (laryngeal nerves); [[★ hypercalcemia]] is its paraneoplastic syndrome
fields.diagnosis: Computed tomography: a large, cavitated lesion with a spiculated outline, nodular inner margins and lymphangitic spread; [[★ unlike the other types, it can be caught by sputum cytology]]; calcium on the metabolic panel
fields.treatment: A combination of surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation (slide 40); slides 37 and 38 title gene-marker targeted therapy and immunotherapy “excluding squamous cell”
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
conditions.prof_note: On his slide 49 list twice: how to recognize small cell, and the cancer that benefits most from radiotherapy (“If the cancer’s pretty limited, you can radiate it really effectively”). Prophylactic cranial irradiation: “We’re literally gonna radiate the brain just in case there’s metastasis.”

fields.name: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC), oat cell carcinoma
fields.definition: A central lung carcinoma that infiltrates the mucosa; limited stage (one area, only local lymph nodes), extensive stage (spread beyond the local area) or combined (mixed with non-small cell types)
fields.etiology: Associated with a lesion of the short arm of chromosome 3; can develop from APUD (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation) cells that secrete polypeptide hormones
fields.epidemiology: 15 to 20% of lung cancers; the type that typically causes the paraneoplastic syndromes
fields.risk_factors: A genetic lesion of the short arm of chromosome 3; the general lung cancer risk factors, smoking above all
fields.pathology: [[★ Central]]; infiltrates the mucosa; a high cavitation rate once large enough for symptoms; histology: a fragile tumor, often crushed at biopsy, with small cells, no nucleoli and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio
fields.clinical: Insidious: [[★ over 70% are metastatic (liver, bone, brain) before detection]]; neuroendocrine paraneoplastic symptoms such as [[★ the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (confusion, seizures, ataxia from a low sodium)]]
fields.diagnosis: Biopsy: crushed small cells with no nucleoli and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio; staged limited or extensive; brain magnetic resonance imaging (preferred over computed tomography) if prophylactic cranial irradiation is planned
fields.treatment: [[★ Responds better to chemotherapy and radiation than the three non-small cell types; radiation works best in limited stage]]. After a complete or partial response, [[★ prophylactic cranial irradiation]] in limited stage, considered (with or without thoracic radiotherapy) in extensive stage; not recommended with poor performance status or impaired neurocognitive function. Immunotherapy is less effective (genetic variability) but becoming an option; two adjunct immunotherapies are approved. Radiotherapy effects: acute skin, mucosa and tissue changes (erythema, hyperpigmentation, ulceration risk), inflammation, hair loss, little nausea; chronic pulmonary fibrosis, cardiovascular damage (coronary artery disease, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy), lymphedema, neuropathy
fields.mortality: Usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis (over 70% before detection); brain metastasis is likely enough that the brain is irradiated prophylactically

fields.name: Lung neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor; bronchial carcinoid
fields.definition: One of the mixed and rare lung cancers; for lung causes, carcinoid syndrome comes mainly only from a bronchial carcinoid
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Release of serotonin from the cancer cells causes the carcinoid syndrome
fields.clinical: Carcinoid syndrome: cutaneous flushes and apparent cyanosis; cough, wheezing, dyspnea; diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting; hepatomegaly; pulmonic and tricuspid valve thickening and stenosis, endocardial fibrosis; retroperitoneal and pelvic fibrosis
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), paraneoplastic
conditions.prof_note: “Small cell lung cancer, you can get SIADH, because that’s real … that patient may show up in the [emergency department] because of the confusion and seizures, and you work it up, and you’re like, oh, that’s lung cancer.”

fields.name: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), a paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer
fields.definition: An endocrine paraneoplastic syndrome: excessive antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) makes the body retain too much water
fields.etiology: [[★ Small cell lung cancer]]: the carcinoma cells develop from neuroendocrine cells in the tumor and produce excess antidiuretic hormone
fields.epidemiology: Patients with small cell lung cancer, the type that typically causes paraneoplastic syndromes
fields.risk_factors: Small cell lung cancer
fields.pathology: Excess antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) causes water retention, hyponatremia and decreased serum osmolality
fields.clinical: [[★ Confusion, seizures, ataxia]] and other neurologic dysfunction, but no signs of peripheral or pulmonary edema, because it develops insidiously
fields.diagnosis: Hyponatremia and decreased serum osmolality (the slides give no diagnostic criteria). A low sodium with high potassium, hypotension, fatigue and dizziness points instead to adrenal insufficiency from a metastasis
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Hypercalcemia, paraneoplastic
conditions.prof_note: “A lot of times, your squamous cell will make your calcium, a big deal.”

fields.name: Hypercalcemia, a paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer
fields.definition: An endocrine paraneoplastic syndrome: a raised calcium from the hormonal or cytokine effects of tumor tissue (the primary or a metastasis)
fields.etiology: [[★ Particularly squamous cell carcinoma]]
fields.epidemiology: Particularly patients with squamous cell lung cancer
fields.risk_factors: Squamous cell lung cancer
fields.pathology: Secreted hormonal or cytokine effects of the tumor tissue (the slides give no more specific mechanism)
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Calcium on the comprehensive metabolic panel in the lung cancer lab workup
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

lectures.title: Pleural Disorders
lectures.note: Built from the slides plus the Zoom recording of the live lecture, which only chooses which facts to star. Slides 34, 58, 60, 74, 83, 97 and 119 are generated pictures with typing errors, read for meaning. He called the procedures a drive-by before the procedures course and said not to memorize the slide 97 laboratory thresholds, chest tube sizes or the flow charts; those are left out. Points the slides state two ways are given both ways or not stated: exactly 3 cm (slides 28, 55, 56), chest tube against aspiration for a large symptomatic primary pneumothorax (slides 55 and 58), tube or needle first in tension (slides 66 and 58), observation and air-leak timings (slides 53, 58, 60), mechanical ventilation as traumatic or iatrogenic (slides 61 and 17), the class of a pulmonary embolism, malignant or chylous effusion (slides 81, 83, 103, 111, 112), the first imaging test for an effusion (slides 90, 95, 97) and how long pleurodynia lasts (slides 118, 119). Current guidelines differ on the needle decompression site, pneumothorax sizing and the hemothorax threshold for thoracotomy; the slides are kept. Where he and a slide differ (pleurodesis, fremitus, the hemothorax film), the slide is kept. Dosing is left out.

fields.name: Pleurisy
fields.definition: Inflammation of the parietal pleura causing pleuritic pain; not a diagnosis but a symptom
fields.etiology: Idiopathic; trauma; infection (bacterial, viral); inflammatory disorders (systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis); pneumothorax; pulmonary embolism; malignancy; drug reactions (methotrexate, amiodarone, hydralazine)
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: The underlying conditions; drugs: methotrexate (chemotherapy), amiodarone (antiarrhythmic), hydralazine (antihypertensive)
fields.pathology: The pleural layers rub together and stimulate pain fibers in the parietal pleura, which has sensory innervation (intercostal and phrenic nerves; the visceral pleura has none); inflammation on the central diaphragm (phrenic nerve) refers pain to the shoulder or neck
fields.clinical: Well-localized sharp or stabbing chest wall pain worse with deep breathing, coughing, movement or sneezing; same-side shoulder or neck pain from the central diaphragm; tachypnea with limited chest wall expansion on the affected side; a pleural friction rub (grating, scratching, creaking; heard in both phases of respiration) that [[★ disappears when the patient holds the breath, unlike a pericardial friction rub]]
fields.diagnosis: Testing depends on the underlying condition. First consider myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism; then rib fracture, costochondritis, vertebral fracture and nerve root pain from herpes zoster
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying condition; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
conditions.prof_note: “I like having a nice, easy number”: the 3 cm apex-to-cupola size; the stability list (“So don’t overthink it”); “don’t confuse gold standard with best initial test”; patient education “may be a question you get.”

fields.name: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
fields.definition: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, with no thoracic trauma and no underlying lung abnormality
fields.etiology: Rupture of apical blebs (under 1 cm, within the visceral pleura) or bullae (over 1 cm, under the visceral pleura), usually at the lung apex; air enters from the lung through the visceral pleura
fields.epidemiology: Classically tall, thin young males, 20 to 40 years of age; male more than female; often at rest, sometimes during strenuous exercise; recurrence is common
fields.risk_factors: Tall, thin young male; smoking (a significant risk factor); family history (inherited association?)
fields.pathology: Pleural pressure is normally negative (about 4 mm Hg below atmospheric), keeping the lung inflated against its tendency to collapse; air from a ruptured bleb or bulla lets the lung collapse. Patients typically have good pulmonary reserve, so severe distress is uncommon
fields.clinical: Acute onset dyspnea and same-side acute pleuritic chest pain (severe, stabbing, worse with deep breathing); may be asymptomatic or only fatigued if small; cough is less common. Exam: tachypnea, tachycardia, decreased chest excursion, decreased or absent tactile fremitus, hyperresonance, diminished or absent breath and voice sounds on the affected side. Differential: myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, dissecting aortic aneurysm, pericarditis, pleurisy, muscle strain, costochondritis
fields.diagnosis: [[★ Initial test: a standard upright chest radiograph]], showing the thin, sharp visceral pleural line, convex toward the chest wall, with no markings beyond it; on a supine film, the deep sulcus sign. [[★ Size by the apex-to-cupola distance: under 3 cm is small]] (American College of Chest Physicians). Point-of-care ultrasound at the bedside (absent lung sliding; it does not size it). [[★ Computed tomography is the gold standard]] for presence, size and location (and finds blebs and bullae) but impractical when time is critical. Arterial blood gas often unnecessary (usually hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis). [[★ Stable only with all of: respiratory rate under 24, heart rate over 60 and under 120, normal blood pressure, room-air oxygen saturation over 90%, speaking in whole sentences]]
fields.treatment: Goals: evacuate the air, close the leak, prevent recurrence. Small (under 3 cm) with minimal symptoms: observation, analgesia, 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask (speeds resorption), a repeat film at 6 to 12 hours, discharge if stable, a film at 24 to 48 hours. Small with significant dyspnea after analgesia: catheter aspiration (2nd intercostal space over the 3rd rib, midclavicular line), Heimlich valve or chest tube; a chest tube for failed observation (enlarging, respiratory rate over 30, saturation under 90%) or failed aspiration. Large (over 3 cm) with moderate or severe symptoms: chest tube (slide 55; the slide 58 picture gives simple aspiration or a small-bore catheter). Recurrent: video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis. [[★ Education: recurrence approaches 50% within three years; the best prevention is video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis; stop smoking]]; delay air travel 7 to 14 days after resolution, confirmed by chest X-ray; avoid scuba diving; early surgical evaluation for pilots and divers; genetics referral for a family history
fields.mortality: Good pulmonary reserve, so severe respiratory distress is uncommon. Recurrence approaches 50% within three years (one-third of primary cases within one to two years; over 60% after a second episode; over 75% of recurrences on the original side)

conditions.name: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
conditions.prof_note: “Your classic board question for … a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is like … tall, skinny, Marfan … 22-year-old”: Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disease, so the pneumothorax is secondary.

fields.name: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
fields.definition: Air in the pleural space with no thoracic trauma but with an underlying lung abnormality; a complication of underlying lung disease
fields.etiology: The underlying disease: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (the most common; rupture of apical blebs), lung malignancy, mesothelioma, cystic fibrosis, pneumonia or tuberculosis, sarcoidosis (interstitial lung disease), [[★ connective tissue disease such as Marfan syndrome]]
fields.epidemiology: Patients with underlying lung disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease most often; in lung malignancy it may be the initial symptom
fields.risk_factors: The underlying lung disease; [[★ Marfan syndrome makes even a tall, thin young man’s pneumothorax secondary]]
fields.pathology: Diminished pulmonary reserve from the underlying disease makes it a more serious event
fields.clinical: The same symptoms as primary, generally greater because of less reserve; an infectious cause adds cough, fever, chills or fatigue; the same physical examination as primary (tachypnea, decreased excursion and fremitus, hyperresonance, diminished breath sounds)
fields.diagnosis: The same imaging (upright chest radiograph first, computed tomography the gold standard, bedside ultrasound); arterial blood gas for severe underlying lung disease or persistent distress (oxygen saturation under 92%) despite treatment
fields.treatment: Most: chest tube insertion. Small (3 cm or less) and asymptomatic: observation, a chest tube for symptoms or a persistent air leak, hospitalization for monitoring. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery or thoracotomy with bleb stapling and pleural abrasion; chemical pleurodesis via chest tube if surgery is not an option. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated with underlying pulmonary disease. Hold positive-pressure therapy during an active air leak
fields.mortality: More life-threatening than primary: diminished reserve requires more immediate intervention; high recurrence rates with greater consequences of recurrence (an indication for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery)

fields.name: Traumatic pneumothorax, closed or open (with iatrogenic pneumothorax)
fields.definition: Pneumothorax with a history of thoracic trauma, blunt or penetrating: closed (no external wound) or open (a wound in the chest wall). Iatrogenic: injury to the pleura from a medical intervention
fields.etiology: Penetrating (gunshot or stab) wound or blunt chest trauma (a rib fracture tears the lung); cardiopulmonary resuscitation; mechanical ventilation (traumatic on slide 61, iatrogenic on slide 17). Iatrogenic: thoracentesis, subclavian vein catheter placement, bronchoscopy
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Chest trauma; medical interventions near the pleura
fields.pathology: Closed: air enters the pleural space from the lung through broken ribs or internal injuries. Open: a direct chest-wall wound lets air in during inhalation and can become a sucking chest wound
fields.clinical: A history of trauma (“Have you had any trauma?”); the presentation depends on the degree of lung collapse; a tension pneumothorax can follow
fields.diagnosis: Bedside point-of-care ultrasound for unstable trauma; computed tomography (the gold standard) for trauma when time allows; upright chest radiograph
fields.treatment: Chest tube (thoracostomy tube; most commonly the 4th or 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line) to drain air or fluid; catheter aspiration is contraindicated in traumatic pneumothorax
fields.mortality: Tension pneumothorax is its life-threatening complication

conditions.name: Tension pneumothorax
conditions.prof_note: Recognize it and act: “At that point, I don’t have to prove it … It is reasonable to act”; his class poll answer was tracheal deviation away from the collapsed lung; the needle site: “For test purposes for now, that would be the right answer.”

fields.name: Tension pneumothorax
fields.definition: A life-threatening complication of pneumothorax in which air enters the pleural space but cannot escape
fields.etiology: A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space; taught as a complication of traumatic pneumothorax
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Traumatic pneumothorax (penetrating or blunt trauma, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, mechanical ventilation)
fields.pathology: Trapped air builds pressure: severe ventilatory compromise, [[★ mediastinal shift to the contralateral side]], decreased venous return to the heart and decreased cardiac output
fields.clinical: [[★ Hypotension, tracheal deviation (away from the collapsed lung) and neck vein distention]]; decreased or absent breath sounds; severe ventilatory compromise
fields.diagnosis: [[★ A clinical diagnosis: time is critical, there is no time for the X-ray]]; the radiographic tension signs (mediastinal shift, diaphragmatic depression) should never be seen before it is recognized
fields.treatment: A medical emergency. Immediate chest tube placement is ideal; if a chest tube is not readily available, immediate needle decompression (needle thoracostomy: [[★ the side of the pneumothorax, 2nd intercostal space, over the 3rd rib, midclavicular line]]; consider body habitus), followed by a moderate or large chest tube (4th or 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line); admission. The slide 58 picture puts urgent needle decompression first, then the chest tube. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated
fields.mortality: Life-threatening: severe ventilatory compromise with falling cardiac output and hypotension

fields.name: Hemothorax (and hemopneumothorax)
fields.definition: Blood in the pleural space: a pleural fluid hematocrit over 50% of the peripheral blood hematocrit (bloody fluid under 50% is a hemorrhagic effusion); strictly an exudative effusion
fields.etiology: Trauma, the most common cause (injury to the heart or vasculature, lung parenchyma, or the intercostal, pulmonary or internal thoracic arteries); neoplasms; iatrogenic (thoracic surgery, invasive procedures); spontaneous vascular disruption; systemic causes (aneurysms, coagulopathies, arteriovenous malformations, endometriosis, neurofibromatosis)
fields.epidemiology: Blunt or penetrating trauma causes the majority; hemopneumothorax occurs in 2 to 3% of spontaneous pneumothoraces
fields.risk_factors: Chest trauma; thoracic surgery or invasive procedures; anticoagulation; coagulopathies
fields.pathology: Blood collects at the base of the pleural space; with air above it (hemopneumothorax) the fluid level is a straight line with no meniscus
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Bedside ultrasound detects pleural fluid rapidly; hemopneumothorax: a straight air-fluid line, no meniscus; an effusion that enlarges during anticoagulation needs thoracentesis to rule out hemothorax; pleural fluid hematocrit over 50% of the blood hematocrit
fields.treatment: Chest tube (typically the 4th or 5th intercostal space, midaxillary line) to evacuate and quantify the bleeding, the essential first step; blood loss over 200 mL per hour: thoracotomy (an open approach); surgery for persistent hemorrhage or hemodynamic shock
fields.mortality: Undrained blood is a nidus for infection; a retained hemothorax leads to empyema, fibrothorax and trapped lung

fields.name: Pneumomediastinum
fields.definition: Air collected in the mediastinal tissues, occurring spontaneously or after procedures or trauma
fields.etiology: Excessive intra-alveolar pressure rupturing alveoli that border the mediastinum; esophageal perforation; esophageal or bowel rupture with air dissecting from the neck or abdomen into the mediastinum
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: A sudden rise in intrathoracic pressure: violent coughing, vomiting, inhalation drug abuse (Valsalva); procedures or trauma
fields.pathology: Air tracks through the mediastinal tissues; the heart beats against air-filled tissue (the Hamman crunch)
fields.clinical: Nonspecific pleuritic chest or neck pain, sore throat, dyspnea, cough; palpable subcutaneous emphysema in the neck; Hamman crunch: substernal crackling or crepitance synchronous with the heartbeat
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Assess and maintain the airway; treat the underlying cause if identified; conservative care (air is gradually absorbed, oxygen may speed absorption, avoid physical activity, analgesics); if severe, an emergent cardiothoracic surgery consult
fields.mortality: Air is often gradually absorbed with conservative care; severe cases need an emergent cardiothoracic surgery consult

conditions.name: Pleural effusion
conditions.prof_note: Light’s criteria: “that makes great test questions” (the slide carries a lightbulb icon); “malignancy and CHF [congestive heart failure] are gonna be your frequent flyers”; of transudates, “Most of it’s gonna be CHF … Like, 90%.”

fields.name: Pleural effusion (transudate or exudate)
fields.definition: Fluid accumulating in the pleural space: an exudate (high protein, from increased vascular permeability) if at least one of Light’s criteria is met, a transudate (low protein, from increased hydrostatic or reduced oncotic pressure) if all are absent
fields.etiology: Altered membrane permeability (inflammation, malignancy); reduced oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminemia: nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis); increased capillary permeability (trauma, malignancy, inflammation, infection); increased hydrostatic pressure (heart failure); decreased or blocked lymphatic drainage (malignancy, trauma); peritoneal fluid crossing the diaphragm (cirrhosis, peritoneal dialysis). Exudates: pneumonia the most common cause, malignancy second (75% breast, lung, lymphoma), tuberculosis the leading cause worldwide. Transudates: [[★ congestive heart failure in over 90%]], cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal dialysis
fields.epidemiology: Over 1.5 million patients a year in the United States; up to 62% of critically ill patients in intensive care; up to 30% have several causes at once; [[★ congestive heart failure is the leading cause]]
fields.risk_factors: Heart failure; cancer (malignant effusions can occur years after the diagnosis); hepatic disease; trauma; asbestos exposure; infection risk factors (diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression, poor dental hygiene); drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, beta blockers)
fields.pathology: Normally about 10 mL of fluid enters from parietal pleura capillaries and leaves by parietal pleura lymphatics, inflow equal to reabsorption; an effusion forms when that balance fails. Adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleurae form loculations (inflammatory causes such as empyema)
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic if small; dyspnea, dry cough and pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse on deep inspiration, referred to the same-side shoulder or upper abdomen). Clues: edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (heart failure); fever, purulent sputum (pneumonia); hemoptysis (malignancy); fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, weight loss (tuberculosis). Exam: no findings under 300 mL; asymmetrical expansion; trachea shifted away over 1000 mL; decreased tactile fremitus; dullness; diminished or absent breath sounds, bronchial toward the top; friction rub
fields.diagnosis: Upright chest radiograph: 75 mL blunts the posterior and 175 mL the lateral costophrenic angle; the lateral decubitus film (effusion side down) has been replaced by ultrasound, which also guides thoracentesis; contrast chest computed tomography finds as little as 10 mL. Diagnostic thoracentesis (50 to 100 mL) for a new effusion with no clinical cause: protein, lactate dehydrogenase, white cell count with differential, Gram stain, cytology, culture; appearance alone is not diagnostic. [[★ Light’s criteria: an exudate if at least one of pleural to serum protein over 0.5, pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase over 0.6, or pleural lactate dehydrogenase over two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase]]
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder (diuretics first for heart-failure transudates); diagnostic or therapeutic thoracentesis (relieves dyspnea and tests whether the lung expands); chest tube; pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions (lung, breast, ovarian) as palliative care, for an expandable lung; an indwelling tunneled pleural catheter, placed as an outpatient and drained at home, for short prognoses, a non-expandable lung or rapidly recurring fluid
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Chylothorax
fields.definition: Accumulation of lipid from chyle (lymph fluid) in the pleural space from thoracic duct disruption
fields.etiology: Trauma, most commonly thoracic surgery; tumors in the mediastinum
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Thoracic surgery or other chest trauma; mediastinal tumors
fields.pathology: Disruption of the thoracic duct, which carries chyle up from the cisterna chyli, lets chyle collect in the pleural space
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Thoracentesis: milky white fluid with elevated triglycerides; with no obvious trauma, a lymphangiogram and computed tomography to assess the mediastinum
fields.treatment: Chest tube or intermittent thoracentesis, avoiding excessive drainage; octreotide (mimics somatostatin, slows gastrointestinal secretions) decreases chyle drainage; fewer long-chain triglycerides in the diet decrease chyle drainage (they are absorbed through the lymphatic system)
fields.mortality: Excessive chyle loss can impair nutritional status

fields.name: Empyema
fields.definition: Purulent fluid in the pleural space
fields.etiology: Bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion, the most common precursor: microorganisms infect the pleural space, causing a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema; a retained hemothorax can also lead to empyema
fields.epidemiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: Pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion; the infection risk factors for effusion (diabetes, alcoholism, immunosuppression, poor dental hygiene); a retained hemothorax
fields.pathology: Pleural inflammation causes adhesions between the visceral and parietal pleurae, forming loculations; fibrin membranes on ultrasound and at thoracoscopy
fields.clinical: Suspect it when pneumonia symptoms do not resolve with therapy; pleuritic pain
fields.diagnosis: Purulent material on thoracentesis
fields.treatment: Prompt therapy is critical: drainage and antibiotics; treat the underlying disease; analgesia for pleuritic pain
fields.mortality: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease)
fields.definition: A viral myalgia of the striated intercostal muscles
fields.etiology: Often coxsackie B virus (an RNA (ribonucleic acid) enterovirus), also echoviruses, typically after an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
fields.epidemiology: Adults (pleuritic pain) and children (abdominal pain); a summer peak; spread by fecal-oral contamination and contaminated water
fields.risk_factors: Exposure to coxsackievirus or echovirus by the fecal-oral route or contaminated water
fields.pathology: The virus targets the striated intercostal muscles, causing inflammation or necrosis and frequent elevations of serum creatine kinase
fields.clinical: Acute onset of fever and pleuritic pain (adults) or abdominal pain (children); paroxysms of severe, knife-like pain lasting 15 to 30 minutes with diaphoresis and tachypnea; splinting of the chest during attacks; tender involved muscles
fields.diagnosis: Elevated serum creatine kinase; a chest radiograph, usually normal, rules out other causes of chest pain
fields.treatment: Supportive: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and heat to the affected muscles; prevention by hand hygiene and pool chlorination
fields.mortality: Symptoms resolve but may recur a few days later; a self-limited, benign course without long-term sequelae; orchitis and aseptic meningitis in under 10%
